To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the shape of the CMB temperature spectrum in a multiple collision scenario is largely model-independent, (2) in a broad class of models, it is characterized by an increase in the quadrupole relative to that of a best-fit $\Lambda CDM$ model, and (3) this predicted spectrum can be used to infer features of the underlying bubble distribution.
the CMB power spectrum in the multiple collision scenario is predicted to be statistically isotropic, but to feature an excess of power in the low multipole region.

the power spectrum of the CMB temperature anisotropies in the presence of multiple cosmic bubble collisions is typically significantly different from the best fit to the $\Lambda$CDMs model and that this feature is largely model independent.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the effects of cosmic collisions on cosmological observables.
the study of multiple collisions between cosmic bubbles of the same or different vacuum states in the context of eternal inflation.
the impact of the collision of multiple cosmic bubbles of different quantum vacua on the cosmic microwave spectrum.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
multiple collisions in the CMB are disfavored at high confidence.
the CMB temperature power spectrum does not rule out the existence of many mild collisions in the history of our Universe.
the CMB power spectrum is not inconsistent with a scenario of many bubble collisions in the past light cone.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the observed low multipoles of the CMB are not in tension with multiple bubble collisions.
multiple collisions are a robust prediction of many false vacuum models, and their effects are potentially observable in the CMB.
the CMB data is consistent with the existence of multiple collisions in the past light cone.
The main takeaway from our work is that

a single collision event is not a good proxy for the expected spectrum from multiple events, and that the latter is much more strongly dependent on the details of the underlying statistical distribution of collisions than the former.
, if multiple collisions occur in an observer's history, the predicted CMB temperature spectrum is likely to be significantly different from that of a single collision.
a multiple collision scenario is a generic feature of eternal inflation scenarios and can be tested observationally.
